title: A failed NCLEX retake study plan on Mac: week by week, for 2026 nurses
metaTitle: Failed NCLEX retake study plan on Mac, 2026 guide
description: Plan your NCLEX retake after failing: the 45-day wait, the score report, closed-book practice and a six-week study plan on Mac.
secondaryKeywords: how to study after failing the NCLEX
intro: To build a failed NCLEX retake study plan, start with the wait and the score report. If your board participates, NCSBN says you can test up to eight times a year, with 45 test-free days between exams. Then change how you study, not only how long you study.
tldr: Your regulatory body sets the real wait. NCSBN's rule is 45 test-free days between exams, and some boards require longer.
Find and read your Candidate Performance Report before you choose a study method.
Switch from rereading to closed-book practice questions with full rationales.
Use spaced repetition for the facts you keep missing, not the whole review book.
Plan around shifts and sleep, and name one person who checks your progress each week.

blocks.text: How long the NCLEX retake wait really is

The official rule is simple, but people misread it. NCSBN's results page says candidates who applied to a participating regulatory body can take the NCLEX up to eight times a year. Between each exam, there must be 45 test-free days. Some regulatory bodies set longer waits, and their rule is the one that applies to you.

Count from your last exam date, not from the day you saw your result. Put the earliest possible date in your Calendar now, and label it as a floor. Your real date may be later. Your board's rules, appointment availability, and your own readiness all count.

blocks.title: Check your board first
blocks.text: Some regulatory bodies set a longer wait than 45 days. Look up your board's rule before you book anything. Write the exact number on your planning sheet.
What a failed NCLEX attempt costs you

The NCSBN results page does not state a retake fee. It sends you to its fees page and to your regulatory body for any fees to test again. Third-party guides often quote a per-attempt price, but no official source confirmed those figures. Check the fees page and your board, then write down the number you find.

If you are not yet licensed, the wait also delays your first paycheck as an RN. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reports a median annual wage of $97,550 for registered nurses in May 2025. Use that as a planning anchor, not a promise. Your state, your employer, and your role change the real number.

The cost people talk about least is emotional. In a 2026 study of nine BSN graduates who failed the NCLEX-RN first and later passed, 88.9% described an emotional impact. They named embarrassment, self-doubt, and social withdrawal. The sample was small and came from one state, so read this as a pattern, not a rate.

Money and jobs pushed many of them to retest. In that study, 55.6% described consequences such as financial strain and delayed employment. The same share, 55.6%, described test-day stress. Those are costs you can plan for, even before you know your score.

items: The retake fee and any board fee, taken from the official fees page
Weeks without a start date or paycheck, based on your board's wait rule
Study hours you can give each week without hurting shifts, sleep, or family time
Money set aside for any review materials you choose to buy
Stress load, since test-day stress and emotional impact both showed up in that study

blocks.text: Why rereading does not fix a failed NCLEX

Most people who fail reread, because it feels productive. In 2006, Roediger and Karpicke tested students with free-recall tests, then checked retention after 5 minutes, 2 days, and 1 week. Students who took memory tests kept substantially more than students who restudied. Restudying left those students more confident, which is why it feels better. The study used prose passages, not NCLEX content.

The 2026 study found a consistent pattern. Every participant changed how they prepared for the retake. The authors call that change the most critical factor in eventual success. Read that as a strong hint, not proof. Nine people, one state, and self-reported memories cannot show which change works best.
Read your Candidate Performance Report first

If you do not pass, NCSBN sends a Candidate Performance Report, or CPR. The results page calls it a guide to prepare for a retake. It does not list what the report contains. Read yours when it arrives instead of guessing. If it opens in Chrome, press ⌘ S and save it to a folder named NCLEX Retake.

Then write three lines. First, the content areas that look weak. Second, the question types that caused trouble, such as select-all-that-apply or prioritization questions. Third, the habit behind your misses, such as rushing or guessing. A long list is hard to act on, so keep it short.
Switch to closed-book practice questions

The fix is simple, though it feels worse at first. Close the review book. Answer a question from memory or from a set of practice questions. Then read the rationale for every option, including the ones you got right. Mark every answer you guessed, even when it was correct.

Say a question about blood glucose trips you up. Do not just reread the insulin chapter. Write the question in your own words, and write why each wrong option is wrong. Make one Anki card for the fact you missed. Then answer three similar questions the next day without notes.

One 2026 study reported that participants who passed on retake followed structured daily schedules and reviewed content in a targeted way. Some did 80 to 100 practice questions per day. Treat that as a reported pattern, not a requirement. Start lower, track your accuracy for a week, then raise the count while your accuracy holds.
Use Anki for the facts you keep missing

Anki is free spaced repetition software. It shows each card again just before you would likely forget it. Use it for facts you missed, not for whole chapters. A card with one fact works better than a card full of paragraphs.

Anki's Mac docs say to download the app from apps.ankiweb.net and drag it into Applications. Homebrew users can run brew install --cask anki in Terminal. The docs say Qt5 builds of version 24.11 and earlier support macOS 10.14 and later. Macs on macOS 10.10 to 10.13 need Anki 2.1.35-alternate. The current version was not checked for this page, so confirm it on the download page first.

items: Open Chrome and go to apps.ankiweb.net.
Download the Mac app and open the downloaded file.
Drag Anki into your Applications folder.
Open Anki once and create a deck for your weakest content area.

Mistakes people make on the second try

items: Rereading the whole outline because it feels safe
Answering hundreds of questions without reading the rationales
Skipping the CPR and guessing your weak areas
Starting Anki with a large batch of new cards, then quitting by week two
Studying late after shifts with no sleep plan
Telling no one, and carrying the stress alone

blocks.text: Support, stress, and your job

The 2026 study authors recommend that schools identify graduates who fail quickly, give them individual study plans, and offer stress-management resources after graduation. Those recommendations are for schools, so you may need to ask for them. Ask a former instructor, a mentor, or a nurse manager for one check-in each week.
Only 33.3% of participants emphasized family, peer, or employer support. The rest focused on other things. Name one person who will ask about your progress each week, and say what you need from them.

If you need time off or a changed schedule for study, draft the request first. Use Outlook or Word for the draft, and keep it factual. Follow your employer's rules on what you can share about your exam and your board. Ask your manager or HR what they expect before you send anything.
Privacy rules for study screenshots and notes

Practice questions often come from a licensed question bank. Read its terms before you share screenshots or copy text outside your own notes. Never paste patient information into study notes, and never screenshot a unit system. Follow your employer's rules on this, even when the study material seems harmless.

Lazur listens and looks at your screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer you. They are not stored, and content is never used to train AI models. Close any patient record on screen before you hold the shortcut.
Where Lazur helps, and where it stops

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac. Hold ⌥⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. Ask where a control is, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it. Ask how to do something, and Lazur guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click.

For this plan, Lazur helps in three places. It can explain a rationale on your screen. You can hold fn and dictate missed-question notes into any app at the cursor. It can set timers for study blocks and Apple Reminders for your board's deadlines.
Lazur does not replace your question bank, your board, or your instructor. It does not click buttons or operate other apps for you. It knows your scores only if they are on your screen.

You can also ask Lazur to research your board's retake rules. Research runs in Lazur's own Chrome tabs, through the Lazur for Chrome extension, and comes back with a summary and a report. Check the board's own page before you rely on the summary.
Next steps this week

Save your CPR in one folder and write the three-line weakness list
Install Anki from apps.ankiweb.net if you plan to use it
Put the earliest test date in your Calendar, labeled as a floor
Start a short closed-book question set tomorrow and log every miss

faq.question: How long do I have to wait to retake the NCLEX?
faq.answer: If your board participates, NCSBN says you can test up to eight times a year, with 45 test-free days between exams. Some boards set longer waits. Your regulatory body's rule is the one to follow.

faq.question: How much does an NCLEX retake cost?
faq.answer: NCSBN's results page does not state a fee. It points you to its fees page and to your regulatory body. Check both before you budget, because third-party guides quote figures that official sources did not confirm.

faq.question: What is the Candidate Performance Report?
faq.answer: Candidates who do not pass receive a Candidate Performance Report. The NCSBN results page calls it a guide to prepare for a retake. The page does not list what the report contains, so read it when it arrives.

faq.question: Should I reread the whole review book before my retake?
faq.answer: Rereading feels productive, but a 2006 study found that restudying gave weaker delayed recall than taking memory tests. That study used prose passages, not NCLEX content. Start with closed-book questions, then reread only the topics you missed.

faq.question: Is Anki free, and does it work on a Mac?
faq.answer: Anki is free to download. Its Mac docs say to get the app from apps.ankiweb.net, or install it with Homebrew using brew install --cask anki. Check the version and macOS requirement on the download page before you install.

faq.question: Can Lazur answer the practice questions for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur answers questions about your screen, points at things, dictates text and guides you through steps. It does not click buttons or operate other apps for you. You still do the questions yourself.

faq.question: Do I have to tell my employer I failed the NCLEX?
faq.answer: Check your employer's policy and your state's rules before you write anything. Ask your manager or HR what they require. Keep any request for time off factual and short.

faq.question: What if my retake wait is longer than 45 days?
faq.answer: Your regulatory body's rule applies. Add the extra days to the later weeks of your plan. Use that time for more closed-book practice, not more rereading.

faq.question: Is 80 to 100 practice questions a day a required target?
faq.answer: No. The 2026 study reported that as what some participants who passed did on retake. It is not a requirement or a proven target. Start lower, track your accuracy, and build up while your results hold.

costs.title: The wait itself
costs.text: NCSBN says candidates can test up to eight times a year, with 45 test-free days between exams. Some boards require longer. Your earliest date may fall weeks after you feel ready, so plan with the wait in mind.

costs.title: A fee you may not know yet
costs.text: NCSBN's results page does not state a retake fee. It points to its fees page and to your regulatory body. Check both. Budget from the official number, not from third-party guesses.

costs.title: Delayed pay if you are not licensed
costs.text: BLS reports a median annual wage of $97,550 for registered nurses in May 2025. A delay in your first RN job means a delay in that income. Use the number as an anchor for your own offer and state.

costs.title: Emotional cost
costs.text: In a 2026 study of nine BSN graduates who later passed, 88.9% described an emotional impact, including embarrassment, self-doubt, and social withdrawal. Plan for that with support and timed practice, not willpower alone.

costs.title: Financial strain and test-day stress
costs.text: The same study found that 55.6% described financial strain and delayed employment as reasons to retest, and 55.6% reported test-day stress. These are the costs that motivated many people to try again.

causes.title: Rereading instead of testing
causes.text: Rereading feels like progress, so many people do more of it after a fail. The 2006 Roediger and Karpicke study found that restudying left people more confident but recalled less on delayed tests. Testing beat rereading, even when the test felt harder.

causes.title: Weak areas guessed, not measured
causes.text: Without reading the CPR or keeping a miss log, people guess their weak areas. Familiar topics feel safe, so study time drifts toward them. The real gaps often stay where they were.

causes.title: A plan that ignores work and sleep
causes.text: The 2026 study found that participants who passed on retake followed structured daily schedules. A plan that ignores shifts, commuting, and sleep is hard to keep. Build the plan around the hours you actually have.

causes.title: Test-day stress and self-doubt
causes.text: The 2026 study reported emotional impact in 88.9% of participants and test-day stress in 55.6%. Stress you never practiced with tends to show up on test day. Practice timed sets before the exam.

causes.title: Little support built into the plan
causes.text: Only 33.3% of participants in the 2026 study emphasized family, peer, or employer support. A plan with no check-in has no one who notices when it slips.

causes.title: Planning around the wrong wait
causes.text: Some people plan around 45 days without checking their board. Some boards set longer waits, and the stricter rule applies. A plan built on the wrong date wastes the early weeks.

fixes.title: Confirm your board's exact wait and fee
fixes.text: Check the NCSBN results page and your regulatory body's website. Write the wait rule, the fee, and the fees page link in one place. Use the stricter rule when you build your plan.

fixes.title: Read your CPR and write a three-line weakness list
fixes.text: Save the CPR when it arrives and read it in full. Write three lines: weak content areas, trouble question types, and the habit behind your misses. Use that list to choose study sessions for the next week.

fixes.title: Practice with closed-book questions and full rationales
fixes.text: Answer from memory first, then read every rationale. Mark guesses and log each miss with one reason. This follows the retrieval practice the 2006 study tested, although that study used prose, not NCLEX content.

fixes.title: Use Anki only for facts you keep missing
fixes.text: Install Anki from apps.ankiweb.net, or run brew install --cask anki in Terminal. Make one card per fact from missed questions. Keep new cards small so daily reviews stay possible on hard days.

fixes.title: Set a weekly check-in and a timed set
fixes.text: Pick one person to review your miss log each week. Add one timed practice set a week to build test stamina. Tell them what you need from the check-in, such as a second look at your weak areas.

fixes.title: Plan the 45 days around work and sleep
fixes.text: Put study blocks in your Calendar around shifts and sleep. Mark rest days on purpose. A plan you can keep for six weeks beats an intense plan you drop by week two.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Find your wait and fee
plan.text: Look up your board's wait rule and fee on its own website. Put the earliest test date in your Calendar as a floor, not a booking.

plan.label: Days 2 to 3
plan.title: Read your CPR
plan.text: Save the CPR when it arrives and read it in full. Write three weak areas and the habit behind each miss, in plain words.

plan.label: Week 1
plan.title: Closed-book baseline
plan.text: Do short closed-book question sets each day. Read every rationale, including the right answers. Log each miss with one reason.

plan.label: Weeks 2 to 3
plan.title: Anki for missed facts
plan.text: Turn missed facts into Anki cards. Keep new cards small. Review on schedule every day, even on short days.

plan.label: Weeks 4 to 5
plan.title: Build volume and timing
plan.text: Raise daily question counts only while accuracy holds. Add one timed set each week and review it the same day.

plan.label: Week 6
plan.title: Rest and logistics
plan.text: Do light review of your weakest cards only. Confirm appointment details and keep your sleep schedule steady. Stop new content early.
